title: Question 4

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by the displacement of the mass on the spring.

markscheme_points.text: distance from a (reference) point in a given direction

hints: Hint 1: Think about where you measure the position from when the mass is just hanging still, and why direction matters as well as distance.
parts.proper_answer: Displacement is the distance from the equilibrium position in a specified direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the Rest Position**
Think of the mass hanging still on the spring before you pull it. That still position is called the equilibrium position. All oscillation measurements are made from there.

Step 2: **Add Distance Plus Direction**
Displacement is not just how far the mass has moved. It is how far from equilibrium, together with which side - above or below, or positive or negative $x$. That is why $x$ in Fig. 4.2 can be positive or negative.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest how Fig. 4.2 shows that the mass is not performing simple harmonic motion.

markscheme_points.text: line is not straight or gradient is not constant

hints: Hint 1: Recall the defining test for SHM on an $a$ against $x$ graph, then look carefully at the shape of Fig. 4.2 at large positive $x$.
parts.proper_answer: For SHM the $a$ against $x$ graph must be a straight line through the origin. Fig. 4.2 curves away from a straight line at large positive $x$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the SHM Signature**
You know SHM is defined by $$a = -\omega^2 x$$ So acceleration must be directly proportional to minus displacement. On an $a$ against $x$ graph that means a straight line with negative gradient passing through the origin.

Step 2: **Spot Where Fig. 4.2 Fails**
Most of Fig. 4.2 is straight, but look at the right-hand end near $x = +1.0\text{ cm}$. The line bends downwards and is no longer straight. Because proportionality fails there, the motion over that full range cannot be simple harmonic.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
The amplitude of oscillation of the mass may be changed.

State the maximum amplitude $x_0$ for which the oscillations are simple harmonic.
hints: Hint 1: Find on Fig. 4.2 the largest positive $x$ value up to which the graph is still a straight line.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Stay Inside the Straight Part**
SHM only holds while the $a$-$x$ graph is straight. The left side stays straight to beyond $x = -1.0\text{ cm}$, but the right side starts to curve at about $x = +0.9\text{ cm}$ where $a \approx -1.1\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Step 2: **Read the Limit**
The amplitude must keep the mass inside the straight section on both sides. So it is limited by the smaller side. Reading off where curvature begins gives $$x_0 \approx 0.90\text{ cm}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: For the simple harmonic oscillations of the mass, use Fig. 4.2 to determine the frequency of the oscillations.
hints: Hint 1: Start from the SHM defining equation $a = -\omega^2 x$ and think what the gradient of the straight part of Fig. 4.2 represents.
Hint 2: Pick two widely separated points on the straight section to find $\Delta a / \Delta x$, remembering to convert $x$ from cm to m.
Hint 3: Use $\omega = 2\pi f$ to go from your value of $\omega^2$ to the frequency $f$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Gradient to Omega**
For SHM $$a = -\omega^2 x$$ So a plot of $a$ against $x$ has gradient $$\text{gradient} = \frac{\Delta a}{\Delta x} = -\omega^2$$ You just need the gradient of the straight part of Fig. 4.2.

Step 2: **Calculate the Gradient**
Choose points well apart on the straight line, for example $x_1 = -0.50\text{ cm} = -0.0050\text{ m}$ with $a_1 \approx +0.65\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $x_2 = +0.50\text{ cm} = +0.0050\text{ m}$ with $a_2 \approx -0.65\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Then $$\omega^2 = -\text{gradient} = -\frac{a_2 - a_1}{x_2 - x_1} \approx -\frac{-0.65 - 0.65}{0.0050 - (-0.0050)} \approx \frac{1.30}{0.010} \approx 130\text{ s}^{-2}$$ This gives $$\omega = \sqrt{130} \approx 11.4\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$

Step 3: **Convert to Frequency**
Use $$\omega = 2\pi f$$ $$f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \approx \frac{11.4}{2\pi} \approx 1.8\text{ Hz}$$

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Think where the speed must be zero and where it must be maximum $v_0$ for oscillation between $+x_0$ and $-x_0$.
Hint 2: Think about the sign of $v$ when the mass travels from $+x_0$ toward $-x_0$, and what curved shape joins those key points.
parts.proper_answer: Lower half of an ellipse from $(+x_0,0)$ through $(0,-v_0)$ to $(-x_0,0)$; $v=0$ at $x=\pm x_0$ and $v=-v_0$ at $x=0$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Mark the Key Points**
At the turning points the mass instantaneously stops, so $v = 0$ at $x = +x_0$ and at $x = -x_0$. At the centre it moves fastest, so $|v| = v_0$ at $x = 0$.

Step 2: **Choose the Correct Half and Shape**
Moving from $+x_0$ to $-x_0$ means $x$ is decreasing, so velocity is negative. The curve therefore lies below the $x$-axis, going from $(+x_0,0)$ down to $(0,-v_0)$ and back up to $(-x_0,0)$. For SHM the $v$-$x$ relation is an ellipse, so this section is the lower semi-ellipse, symmetric about $x = 0$.
